title: Finding humanity – and hope – in the world’s grasslands
text:
Finding humanity – and hope – in the world’s grasslands
With the vast majority of the world’s population living in urban areas, few people have met a true-blue pastoralist. But the lands these nomads steward matter to us all.
The world’s grasslands – or rangelands, or savannas, or any of the other terms people use to describe a good quarter of the Earth’s surface – might not get the same attention as its forests. But these ecosystems sink nearly as much carbon. They offer food security and economic benefits. And they provide a livelihood to millions of pastoralists around the globe.
These nomadic herders don’t usually make headlines, either. But they and their lifestyles hold significant importance – not just for cultural reasons, but for ecological ones.
Well-managed rangelands are “one of the best climate adaptation strategies we have,” says Marcy Vigoda, director of the International Land Coalition. Ms. Vigoda works with governments and grassroots groups in dozens of countries to try to advance Indigenous and pastoral land rights. Data shows that in areas where pastoralists’ land rights are more secure, grasslands are generally healthier and more productive.
I talked to Ms. Vigoda while editing two of the pieces we highlight on this week’s cover, from countries where pastoralism is a core part of the national identity. As the Asia editor at the Monitor, I am regularly looking for stories like these; stories that open readers to the larger trends and thought shifts that are happening outside of the daily news cycle.
In a dispatch from Kyrgyzstan, photographer and writer Michael Benanav documents how young pastoralists from around the world come together to brainstorm solutions to the problems facing their communities back home, including a lack of internet and cell connectivity.
In Mongolia, writer and photographer Randall Hyman introduces us to six citizens trying to navigate the booming demand for mining in traditional Gobi Desert rangelands.
Pastoralists face several existential challenges, from misinformation and stereotypes to climate change and land encroachment. But both of the stories this week provide reasons to be hopeful. And Ms. Vigoda sees another.
A decision reached at the United Nations’ annual conference on desertification (COP17), held in Ulaanbaatar this August, highlighted the importance of protecting pastoralists’ seasonal migration routes. It recognized “not only mobility within a country, but transboundary mobility, which I never thought would be agreed,” she says. “These decisions at COPs are nonbinding, but they give you the foundation to try to drive forward policy change. ... It’s super, super positive. And Mongolia played a big role in that.”
